title: Grounds for Dependency (WIC Section 300)
before: The child is suffering serious emotional damage, evidenced by severe anxiety, depression, withdrawal, or aggressive behavior toward self or others.
after: The child has serious emotional harm, or is at big risk of it, because of what the parent did, or because no parent is able to give the right care. Signs are severe anxiety, depression, withdrawal, or aggressive behavior.

title: Grounds for Dependency (WIC Section 300)
before:
Section 300(g) - No Parental Custody
The child has been left without provision for support and the parent cannot be located.
after:
Section 300(g) - No One to Care for the Child
Any one of these: the child was left with no support. Or the child was safely surrendered as a newborn and not taken back in 14 days. Or the parent is in jail or an institution and cannot arrange care. Or the adult caring for the child cannot keep doing it and the parent cannot be found.

title: Grounds for Dependency (WIC Section 300)
before: The child has been freed for adoption but placement has not been finalized.
after: The child has been freed for adoption by one or both parents for 12 months, or an adoption petition has not been granted.

title: Grounds for Dependency (WIC Section 300)
before: Section 300(i) - Cruelty (Criminal)
after: Section 300(i) - Cruelty

title: Grounds for Dependency (WIC Section 300)
before: Section 300 is the law that explains why CPS can take your child or start a court case.
after: Section 300 is the law that lists the reasons the county can start a court case about your child. To take a child without a court order, the social worker must also believe the child is in danger right now.

title: JV-180: Request to Change Court Order
before: 4. Serve a copy on the county and your child's attorney
after: 4. Everyone in the case has to get a copy. If you have a lawyer, your lawyer sends the copies. If you do not have a lawyer, the court clerk sends them for you.

title: JV-180: Request to Change Court Order
before: You need to show two things: (1) circumstances have changed, and (2) the change you are asking for is in the best interest of your child.
after: You need to show two things: (1) something has changed, or there is new information the judge did not have, and (2) the change you want is good for your child.

title: How to Request Your Case File
before: - DCFS/CPS assessment and investigation reports
after: - County assessment and investigation reports that were filed with the court. Some parts may be kept private unless a judge orders them released.

title: How to Request Your Case File
before: Your attorney can submit a written response to the court correcting the record.
after: If you do not agree with a report, call your lawyer right away and go to your next court date. Your lawyer can tell the judge what is wrong.
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY, but the record's fix gives wording its steps tie to the Judicial Council booklet.

title: How to Request Your Case File
before: Welfare & Institutions Code § 827; California Rules of Court, Rule 5.552
after: Welfare & Institutions Code § 827(a)(1)(D), (a)(5) (a parent's right to see and copy the file); California Rules of Court, Rule 5.552 and form JV-570 (only for people who are not already allowed to see the file, or for parts a judge must release)
note: Record lists field full_content but the statement is the legal_reference and external_link values. Rule 5.552 kept, now scoped the way the fix says.

title: How to Request Your Case File
before: https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/jcc-form/JV-570
note: The record also questions the external_link to JV-570. external_link is a column outside the allowed fields and the fix gives no replacement link, so it was left as is. A parent tapping the link still lands on the JV-570 petition page.

title: If You Want to Be Included in Your Child's Case
before: Your name is on the birth certificate, you were married to the birth parent, a family court named you a parent, or you raised the child as your own.
after: You were married to the birth parent, a family court named you a parent, or you raised the child as your own. You may also be a presumed parent if you signed a voluntary declaration of parentage. Being named on the birth certificate may count too. Ask a lawyer.
note: Birth certificate claim moved out of the list and reworded per the fix; the rest of the sentence was only reordered so it reads cleanly.

title: If You Want to Be Included in Your Child's Case
before: You were married to the birth parent, a family court named you a parent
after: You were married to the birth parent when the child was conceived or born, a family court named you a parent
note: Applied after record f881a3039f9a changed the same sentence.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: If your child may be a member of, or eligible for membership in, a federally recognized Indian tribe, the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) provides special protections.
after: If your child is a member of a federally recognized tribe, or can be a member and has a birth parent who is a member, the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) gives special protections.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: - Placement preferences favor Native family members and tribal members
after: - Placement rules put the child's family first, even family members who are not Native. Next come homes the tribe approves and other Native homes.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: - Your attorney should file to invoke ICWA protections
after: - You do not have to file anything to get ICWA protections. The court and the county must ask about it and look into it. The judge will have you fill out form ICWA-020 about your family's tribal ties. Tell your lawyer so they can make sure this gets done.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: - The tribe may appoint a representative to assist you
after: - The tribe can send someone to speak for the tribe in court. The tribe may also have services that can help your family.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: Common tribes in California: There are 109 federally recognized tribes in California. If you have heritage from any of them, ICWA may apply.
after: ICWA covers every federally recognized tribe in the United States, not just the 109 in California. If your child is tied to any of them, ICWA may apply.

title: ICWA-030: Notice of Child Custody Proceeding for Indian Child
before: If you or your child has any Native American heritage, you have special rights called ICWA protections. Tell your lawyer and the court even if you are not sure.
after: If you or your child may have Native American ancestry, tell your lawyer and the court, even if you are not sure. If your child is a member of a tribe, or can be a member and has a parent who is one, special rules called ICWA protect your family.
note: The fix already includes the 'tell your lawyer and the court' sentence that followed, so both sentences were swapped to avoid saying it twice.

title: JV-290: Caregiver Information Form
before: (foster parents, relatives, group home representatives)
after: (foster parents, relatives, preadoptive parents, or a community care facility or foster family agency caring for the child)
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY for 'group home'; the fix wording comes from form JV-290 per the record's steps.

title: JV-290: Caregiver Information Form
before: It covers the child's health, education, behavior, relationship with family, and any concerns.
after: It covers the child's health, school, how the child is adjusting to the home, friends and social skills, interests and activities, other helpful information, and what you think should happen next.

title: JV-290: Caregiver Information Form
before: Fill it out before review hearings.
after: Turn it in to the court clerk at least 5 calendar days before a review or permanency hearing. If you mail it, send it at least 7 calendar days before.

title: JV-290: Caregiver Information Form

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
before: - Must be held within 60 days of the detention hearing
after: - If your child was removed, the disposition hearing is usually held within 10 court days after the jurisdiction hearing. Delays should not push it past 60 days after the detention hearing. A judge can go past 60 days only for very unusual reasons, and never past 6 months.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
before: - Judge determines if the allegations are true and if the child should be declared a dependent
after: - The judge decides if what the petition says is true. If it is true, the court takes authority over your child. The formal dependency order is made at the disposition hearing.
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY because two sources differ; the fix wording follows WIC 360(d) as quoted in the record's steps. Whole bullet swapped; 'At the jurisdiction hearing' left off because the bullet sits under that heading.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
before: - If reunification fails, this hearing establishes a permanent plan (adoption, guardianship, or long-term foster care)
after: - If reunification fails, this hearing sets a permanent plan. The choices are adoption, tribal customary adoption, guardianship, living with a fit and willing relative, or staying in foster care with a plan.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
before: and situations where a parent cannot care for a child because of drug or alcohol problems.
after: and cases where a child was badly hurt or sick, or is at serious risk of that, because a parent cannot give regular care due to drug or alcohol problems.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
before: Must show changed circumstances AND best interest of child
after: Must show changed circumstances or new evidence, AND that the change is best for the child

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
before: - The judge, commissioner, or referee, who runs the hearing and decides
note: The fix is not wording ('No change needed if a source for commissioners is added on a later check'). Only the word 'commissioner' is unverified; judge and referee are confirmed. Text left as is.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
before: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 358
after: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 16501.1 (what a case plan is); § 358(b) (the plan goes in the court report); § 388 (asking for changes)

title: What Happens at Detention Hearing
before: Dress neatly, arrive 30 minutes early, bring ID
after: Dress neatly and get to court early so you have time to check in.

title: What Happens at Detention Hearing
before: Hearing is usually brief (15-30 minutes). Focus is on immediate safety
after: The hearing is often short. The judge looks at whether your child can safely go home right away.

title: What Happens at Detention Hearing
after: WIC §319; Cal. Rules of Court, rules 5.534, 5.668, 5.670, 5.674

title: When the Case Closes: Dismissal and Exit Orders
before: If your child will live with one parent and the parents are not together, the judge makes exit orders when closing the case.
after: If your child will live with one parent and the parents are not together, the judge can make exit orders when closing the case. Ask your lawyer if the judge will make one in your case.
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY because sources differ on 'will' versus 'may'; the fix wording follows WIC 362.4(a) as quoted in the record's steps.

title: When the Case Closes: Dismissal and Exit Orders
before: If the parents live apart, the judge makes a custody order that stays in place.
after: If the parents live apart, the judge can make a custody order. That order stays in place until a family court judge changes it.
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY because sources differ; the fix wording follows WIC 362.4(a),(b) as quoted in the record's steps.

title: Your Rights at the Detention Hearing
before: The county must tell you what they are alleging and why they removed your child.
after: The judge must tell you what the petition says and why your child was removed.
note: COULD_NOT_VERIFY for the county's duty; the fix wording follows rule 5.668(a) as quoted in the record's steps.

title: Your Rights at the Detention Hearing
before: 5. Right to visitation: Unless there are safety concerns, you have the right to visit with your child.
after: 5. Visits: The judge must look at visits at this hearing. The judge decides if contact is good or harmful for your child and then makes visit orders. Ask your lawyer to ask for visits.

title: Your Rights at the Detention Hearing
before: 8. Right to Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) protections: If you or your child has Native American heritage, special protections apply.
after: 8. Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) protections: These apply if your child is a member of an Indian tribe, or can be a member and has a birth parent who is a member. Only the tribe decides this. Tell the judge and your lawyer right away about any tribal ties so they can check.
note: Kept the spelled-out name of ICWA in the label.

title: Your Rights at the Detention Hearing
before: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 319
after: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 319; Cal. Rules of Court, rules 5.530, 5.534, 5.668, 5.670, 5.674; 25 U.S.C. § 1903(4)

title: Your Visitation Order
before: - Holiday and birthday visit schedules
after: - Holiday or birthday visits, but only if the judge adds them. Ask your lawyer to ask for them.

title: Your Visitation Order
before: - Talk to your social worker first — they can sometimes adjust visits informally
after: - Tell your social worker and your lawyer what change you want. Ask your lawyer to bring it to the judge.

title: Your Visitation Order
before: - Visitation is your right unless the court finds it would be detrimental to your child
after: - If the judge ordered reunification services for you, the judge must also order visits with your child. No visit order can put your child's safety at risk.

title: Your Visitation Order
